b.text:
LUBANG, A PATH IN I THE JUNGLE
FEBRUARY 20, 1974

Night lets go of me slowly. The fever-dream thins rather than ends, and what replaces it is no kinder: daylight the color of wet slate, a jungle that seems to switch itself on and off. Somewhere beyond the ridge, clouds are working themselves into a rage, and the light below them stutters, goes pale, returns, as if the whole island were wired to a faulty circuit. The trees take each flash like a blow they have learned not to flinch from. Thunder is promised but never delivered; it stays out at sea, mute, withheld. Only the rain arrives, steady and indifferent, falling as though it had been falling for thirty years.
Am I awake? Is this the dream, or the thing the dream was hiding?
A path of red clay, slick as a skinned animal. Nothing on it. Then voices.
A young man comes running, barefoot, splashing. In one hand a bolo, its blade dull with rain. In the other, the bare wire ribs of an umbrella, the cloth long gone, held aloft like a trophy or a warning. Behind him a woman with a baby pressed against her chest, and three, four others, talking over one another, half laughing, half alarmed. Why the hurry, nobody says; they are gone before anyone could ask.
The path empties. The trees drip, each leaf passing its drop to the leaf below.
Stillness again. Long enough to believe in.
Then the wall of green beside the path shifts. Not wind. A section of foliage leans, hesitates, and becomes a shape. A man, or something deciding to be one. He has been standing there the whole time, so close the villagers could have touched him.
He is in his early fifties, lean to the point of wire, every muscle drawn tight beneath skin the color of the clay. His uniform is no longer a uniform but an argument of patches, scrap stitched to scrap by his own hand. He peels away the leaves and twigs bound to his arms and shoulders, one by one, unhurried, the way another man sheds a coat. He reaches into the brush and draws out a rifle, its butt wrapped in strips of bark, then a rucksack, dark with damp. He listens. He does not move. Then he follows the villagers down the path, placing each foot where the clay will not speak.
Hiroo Onoda. Lieutenant. Still at war.
A dream, then? I have pictured it so often that I can no longer tell.
After he has gone, I stay and listen as he would. A bird calls, twice, and the calling means: no one is near. Insects resume their electric hum, which means: the danger has moved on. A stream below rushes on, meaning nothing at all, the best news the jungle can give. The rain, too, is forgiven. The jungle is becoming a language, and I am starting to read it the way he does.

a.text:
Questions About Angels

Not the large ones. Somebody has already asked
 about suffering, and the war in heaven, and whether
 the trumpet will be a trumpet or more of a feeling.
 Those are on file. Those have a waiting list.

I want to know if the halo comes off at night
 and where it goes, a hook by the door, a dish
 on the dresser with the loose change of the saved.

I want to know if wings itch where they join the back,
 and whether there’s a long-handled brush for that,
 or a colleague, or simply an eternity of bearing it.

I want to know what they do with Tuesday,
 if they have Tuesday, if anything up there
 is ever returned to a shelf slightly out of order.

I want to know whether they dream, and if the dreams
 are of falling, the way ours are of flying,
 some seraph jolting awake in a sweat of light
 having spent the night as a man late for a bus.

I want to know if one of them, by clerical error,
 has ever been posted to a parking garage in Dayton,
 handing tickets through the little window,
 saying have a good one in the voice
 that once told shepherds not to be afraid.

But I suspect that if one stood in my kitchen,
 ducking the light fixture, dripping glory on the linoleum,
 I would forget the list, and offer coffee,
 and it would be the angel who had questions.

What is it like to be tired. Why do you keep
 the photographs in a drawer and the bills on the table.
 What are you doing when you stand at the open
 refrigerator, looking in, taking nothing.

And I would say I don’t know, I’ve always done that,
 and it would nod, and write this down
 on whatever they write things on,
 and ask if it could please try the door itself.

b.text:
Pants on Fire

By the end of third grade, I owned a palomino named Duchess, a second cousin who played for the Lakers, and a basement with a working volcano. Only the basement was real, and it did not have a volcano. It had a dehumidifier.

My lies began, as most fires do, with a spark and a draft. The draft came from the window table at Hillcrest Elementary, where the popular third graders ate beneath a slab of afternoon sun. I sat at the next table over, at the very end of the bench, where the light stopped exactly one seat short of me, as if it had been rationed. From there I could hear them trading Gushers and weekend stories, and I could see that the sun fell only on people with something to say.

So I struck a match. One Tuesday, over a tray of rectangular pizza, I leaned across the gap and mentioned Duchess. Kaitlyn Moreno turned around. By Friday I had a seat in the sun.

A fire, I discovered, is not something you start once. It is something you feed. Duchess required a stable, then a blue ribbon, then a tragic leg injury I narrated across several lunches like a serialized Victorian novel. My cousin required a championship ring and a signed jersey that was, regrettably, at the dry cleaner. Each morning on the bus I gathered kindling, rehearsing new particulars, and each lunch I stoked the blaze a little higher. I was eight and already a full-time fabulist, curating an apocrypha more intricate than most fantasy franchises.

I understood the stakes with perfect clarity. If the fire went out, the sun would go with it. Kaitlyn would stop saving me the seat by the window. The Gushers would travel past me down the table. When teams were picked for four square, I would be chosen after the boy who still wore light-up sneakers. I would return to the end of the bench, where it was cold, and everyone would know I had been nobody impersonating somebody.

Then, one gray Monday in March, Danny Okafor sat down at the window table with a thermos and said, “My weekend was so boring.”

I waited for the silence to swallow him.

“I helped my dad clean the gutters,” he continued, unscrewing the lid. Steam rose, smelling of chicken soup. “And we found a dead bird. Like, a whole bird. With feathers.”

Kaitlyn set down her juice box. “Wait. What kind?”

“I don’t know. Brown?”

“Did you touch it?” someone asked. “Did you bury it?” asked someone else. Danny explained that they had buried it under the hydrangeas, that his little sister had insisted on a funeral, and that she had sung the only song she knew all the words to, which was the theme from Paw Patrol. The table laughed so hard that Marcus Lee shot milk out of his nose. Nobody asked about Duchess.

I watched the Gushers drift toward Danny, one packet at a time.

On Thursday, Danny was still at the window table, describing his orthodontist appointment in unremarkable detail. Everyone wanted to know whether it hurt.

The following Monday, Kaitlyn asked about my weekend, and I left the matches in my pocket. I told her it was boring. I told her our basement had flooded and my dad and I had spent Saturday bailing water with mixing bowls. I told her I’d found our Monopoly board floating past the dehumidifier like a raft. She laughed and asked whether the money survived.
Duchess, I announced shortly thereafter, had retired to a farm upstate.
